title: IRD’s Rs. 500,000 cash rule: Cost not crime for individuals, companies | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:56
-     - 1603

Individuals and companies that make payments of Rs. 500,000 or more in cash outside approved banking channels can face a sharp rise in their tax bills, a tax expert said. He was clarifying recent television comments by Inland Revenue Department (IRD) Commissioner Sudath Gunathilake. Clips of the interview have been circulating on social media and have caused a stir and raised several concerns.

Gunathilake said cash transactions exceeding Rs. 500,000 could result in higher tax liabilities. This included payments for land, property and vehicles.

“A common misconception is that paying Rs. 500,000 or more in cash is a criminal offence or invalidates a commercial contract. In reality, Section 10(2A) imposes a strict financial penalty through the tax system,” KPMG Sri Lanka Principal and Head of Tax and Regulatory, Attorney-at-Law Suresh Perera explained to Daily FT.

Under the provision, such payments are disallowed in full as tax-deductible expenses and cannot be counted as part of an asset’s acquisition cost, Perera said. A company paying the standard 30% corporate income tax rate that settles a Rs. 1 million bill in cash would add Rs. 300,000 directly to its tax bill.

For an investor who buys land for Rs. 90 million in cash and later sells it for Rs. 100 million, the IRD disregards the purchase price. Capital Gains Tax is then charged on the entire Rs. 100 million sale value rather than the Rs. 10 million profit. Businesses also lose capital allowances, the annual tax deduction for depreciation, on machinery or vehicles bought with cash above the limit.

KPMG Sri Lanka Principal and Head of Tax and Regulatory Suresh Perera

Splitting payments does not get around the rule either. “Taxpayers cannot bypass the rule by breaking a single bill into smaller cash vouchers,” Perera said. Payments to the same recipient that total Rs. 500,000 or more within a single day, or across several instalments for a single transaction or event, are added together and disallowed in full.

Taxpayers can protect their deductions and asset cost claims by paying through one of six approved methods. These are account payee cheques crossed “Account Payee Only”, as open or bearer cheques do not qualify, account payee bank drafts, credit cards and debit cards. 

Electronic bank transfers also qualify, whether through the Common Electronic Fund Transfer Switch (CEFTS), the Sri Lanka Interbank Payment System (SLIPS), Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS), or online and mobile banking. The sixth method is a direct cash deposit into the recipient’s bank account. Payments made to or by the Government of Sri Lanka, State institutions, banks and licensed financial institutions are exempt.

The deposit option was added only this year. “The original 2023 law created an unexpected hurdle: businesses that deposited physical cash over the counter directly into a supplier’s bank account risked tax disallowances, even though the transaction left a clear bank trail,” Perera said.

Parliament fixed this in June 2026 through the Inland Revenue (Amendment) Act, No. 11 of 2026, which explicitly recognises direct deposits into a recipient’s account as a valid payment method. The change applies retrospectively from 8 May, 2023, as explained in IRD Notice SEC/PN/IT 2026/02.

Budget 2027, presented to Parliament on 12 November, builds on that reform. Under a proposal set to take effect on 1 April, 2027, the Commissioner General of Inland Revenue (CGIR) will accept a formal certificate from an “approved accountant” or “authorised person”. The certificate will confirm that high-value payments went through approved banking channels, giving third-party verification of compliance with Section 10(2A).

“Until now, proving compliance with the five-lakh rule relied heavily on post-filing tax audits by IRD officers. This often left businesses facing prolonged uncertainty over whether legitimate expenses would be questioned years later,” Perera said.

“By shifting frontline verification to independent accounting professionals, the Budget 2027 proposal aims to speed up tax assessments, reduce audit bottlenecks and curb disguised cash transactions,” he added.

Under the Inland Revenue Act, an approved accountant for all companies must be a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Sri Lanka (CA Sri Lanka). The same applies to individuals and partnerships with an annual turnover exceeding Rs. 100 million. For individuals and partnerships with a turnover of Rs. 100 million or less, a CA Sri Lanka member or a Fellow Member of AAT Sri Lanka qualifies. The CGIR will also be empowered to designate additional authorised persons and set the official certificate format ahead of the 2027/28 year of assessment.

Perera said Sri Lankan tax law placed no general limit on settling business expenses in cash before 2023. Section 10(2A) was inserted into the Inland Revenue Act, No. 24 of 2017 on 8 May, 2023, as part of wider fiscal reforms to bring the informal cash economy into the tax net.

title: Registrar of Companies’ online system breakdown leaves businesses in limbo | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:52
-     - 250

The country’s corporate regulatory system has been thrown into disarray after the Registrar of Companies (RoC) online platform, the central portal for company registrations, statutory filings and compliance submissions, ground to a complete halt, leaving thousands of businesses unable to file or carry out essential corporate transactions.

Industry sources told the Daily FT that the platform has remained non-functional for several days, with the disruption.

The shutdown has effectively paralysed routine corporate processes, including new company incorporations, annual returns, amalgamations, company closures and changes to company directors. Businesses are also struggling to meet statutory compliance deadlines, potentially exposing them to legal and regulatory complications.

“At this point, this goes beyond a technical failure. It has become a serious business continuity issue with the operations of thousands of companies affected,” sources said, raising concerns over institutional accountability, management and the absence of effective communication with stakeholders.

Industry representatives claimed the ROC was neither accepting manual submission nor facilitating in-person transactions as an alternative to the disabled online system.

The impact is particularly concerning for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), which depend on timely company filings to secure banking facilities, obtain regulatory approvals and conclude investor agreements. Larger companies are also affected with mergers, capital restructuring and Board appointments among the transactions facing disruption. 

Despite several attempts to contact RoC Commissioner General or other officials were not available for comment.

Businesses said the absence of an alternative filing mechanism had left them with no means of completing mandatory submissions or progressing essentials corporate transactions. A corporate lawyer warned that the disruption was already creating uncertainty over compliance obligations, with companies facing the prospect of missing statutory deadlines despite being unable to access the system.

title: Budget 2027 to stimulate business and jobs: Treasury | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:52
-     - 158

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma

The 2027 Budget’s Rs. 2 trillion allocation for capital expenditure is expected to stimulate the business sector, improve profitability and create jobs, Secretary to the Treasury Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma said. Capital expenditure is spending on infrastructure and other long-term assets.

Dr. Suriyapperuma was speaking on 19 November, 2026 at a post-Budget dialogue organised by the Association of International Certified Professional Accountants (AICPA) and the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants (CIMA) Sri Lanka. The theme was “The 2027 Budget and Beyond: Navigating the Future of Business and Growth”.

He said the Budget builds on the economic policy approach adopted in 2025 and 2026. He described its aim as sustaining economic stability while creating conditions for business growth, investment and job creation, and strengthening the confidence of businesses, citizens and investors.

On revenue, he said the Government will not raise tax rates. Instead it will broaden the tax base, which means bringing more people and activities into the tax net. It will also strengthen revenue collection and use digitalisation to improve efficiency. The Government expects these measures to gradually bring informal economic activity into the formal economy and to make it easier for businesses and citizens to deal with the State.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said Rs. 174 billion has been allocated in 2027 to support Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). The support is expected to help them build capacity, adopt new technology and machinery, access consultancy services and expand into export markets.

He said public investment projects are now being identified and funded through a more systematic process. Projects are prioritised on their readiness and feasibility, their economic impact and the value they add to the economy.

He added that cooperation between the public and private sectors is essential to make the economy more resilient to external shocks, build economic buffers and ensure fiscal stability. Economic buffers are reserves that help the economy absorb sudden shocks.

The panel included Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe, John Keells Holdings Group Finance Director Gihan Cooray, Advocata Institute CEO Dhananath Fernando and KPMG Sri Lanka Chief Tax and Regulatory Officer Suresh R.I. Perera.

title: National reconciliation essential for economic take-off: NPC | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:51
-     - 49

The National Peace Council (NPC) has said that the 2027 Budget lacks a clear commitment and budgetary provision for holding Provincial Council elections, and that proposals to transfer provincial hospitals to central Government control run counter to the need to strengthen decentralised governance. The full statement issued by its Governing Council follows:

The Government’s 2027 Budget draft sets out an extensive program for economic recovery, stabilisation and national development. The National Peace Council (NPC) recognises the importance of these objectives, including combating corruption, improving public services and restoring confidence in the economy. However, the absence of a clear commitment and budgetary provision for holding Provincial Council elections, together with proposals to transfer provincial hospitals to central Government control, raises concerns about the direction of Government policy. These developments run counter to the need to strengthen decentralised governance and bring decision-making closer to the people.

The NPC appreciates the Government’s commitment to national reconciliation as reflected in its development initiatives in the North and East. The 2027 Budget provides significant financial allocations towards resettling families displaced by the conflict, developing fisheries infrastructure in the Northern Province and implementing water supply projects in the northern and eastern districts. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s stated commitment to building a just society in which every citizen has the opportunity to enjoy a decent life and share equitably in economic progress is also welcome. The Government’s commitment to equality and action against extremism in all its forms provides an important foundation for national reconciliation.

The National People’s Power (NPP) Government came to office with an unprecedented mandate for system change and a promise to break with the divisive politics and governance failures of the past. However, a development strategy that concentrates authority at the centre, rather than building the capacity of local and provincial institutions, risks perpetuating the inequalities and alienation that reconciliation must overcome. The devolution of power in a multi-ethnic and multi-religious country is an essential component of democratic governance. Empowering provincial institutions can improve accountability, make public services more responsive to local needs and enable communities to participate meaningfully in decisions affecting their lives.

The Government’s commitments to equality and reconciliation need to translate into practical action on the ground. The longstanding dispute over the Mayilathamadu-Mathavanai grazing lands in Batticaloa illustrates this challenge. The occupation of traditional grazing lands by settlers under the centralised Mahaweli program has adversely affected local cattle farmers, despite assurances given by successive Presidents, including President Dissanayake. The Government needs to resolve this dispute, protect the livelihoods and grazing rights of local farmers and ensure that land settlement respects constitutional and legal principles.

The NPC calls on the Government to demonstrate its commitment through practical measures, including strengthening devolution of power, holding Provincial Council elections, addressing the concerns of families of the disappeared, returning military-occupied land to its rightful owners and engaging in meaningful dialogue with minority political representatives and civil society. These are not competing priorities or additional burdens on the national Budget. They are investments in democratic stability, public trust, social cohesion and economic development. Sri Lanka cannot achieve its full potential while its deepest historical divisions remain unresolved.

The National Peace Council is an independent and non-partisan organisation that works towards a negotiated political solution to the ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka. It has a vision of a peaceful and prosperous Sri Lanka in which the freedom, human rights and democratic rights of all the communities are respected. The policy of the National Peace Council is determined by its Governing Council of 20 members who are drawn from diverse walks of life and belong to all the main ethnic and religious communities in the country.

title: NCPI inflation climbs to 8.5% in Oct. | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:51
-     - 108

National inflation accelerated to 8.5% year-on-year (YoY) in October 2026 from 8.1% in September, as both food and non-food prices rose faster. The figures come from National Consumer Price Index (NCPI) data released by the Department of Census and Statistics (DCS) on Monday.

The reading ends a one-month pause in the climb. YoY inflation held at 8.1% in September after rising every month from 1.6% in February. A year earlier, in October 2025, it stood at 2.7%.

The NCPI (Base: 2021=100) rose to 225.1 points in October from 224.2 in September. The month-on-month (MoM) increase of 0.9 index points, or 0.41%, was the largest monthly rise since July. It corresponds to a rise of Rs. 466.07 in the expenditure value of the market basket, against Rs. 123.85 in September.

The 12-month moving average, which compares the average index over the past 12 months with that of the preceding 12 months, rose to 5% from 4.5%.

Food inflation rose to 7.2% YoY from 6.9%. Non-food inflation reversed its September easing and climbed to 9.5% from 9.1%. Non-food items contributed 5.29 percentage points to the headline rate, against 3.21 percentage points from food.

Transport remained the biggest single contributor, adding 2.45 percentage points, up from 2.20 percentage points in September. Petrol alone accounted for 1.21 percentage points, followed by Bus Fare (0.36), Diesel (0.20) and Transport for Schooling/Preschooling (0.19). 

Housing, Water, Electricity, Gas and Other Fuels added 1.17 percentage points, led by Housing Rent (0.46), Materials for Maintenance (0.30) and L.P. Gas (0.23). Restaurants and Hotels (0.52), Education (0.39) and Miscellaneous Goods and Services (0.26) also contributed.

On the food side, the annual increase was driven by Vegetables (0.79 points), Fresh Fish (0.47), Dried Fish (0.40), Big Onions (0.38) and Milk Powder (0.26). Declines in Coconuts (-0.48), Rice (-0.32) and Limes (-0.07) partly offset these gains.

On a MoM basis, non-food items added 0.33% to the index, led by Petrol (0.15%) and Tuition Fees (0.05%), while food items added 0.08%. Within food, increases in Vegetables (0.25%), Limes (0.20%) and Milk Powder (0.07%) were largely offset by lower prices for Fresh Fish (-0.27%) and Green Chillies (-0.16%).

The data come days after the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) raised its Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) by 25 basis points to 9%. It was the second hike this year, after a 100 basis point increase in May. The Standing Deposit Facility Rate and the Standing Lending Facility Rate, which are linked to the OPR, rose to 8.50% and 9.50%, respectively. 

The CBSL also raised the Statutory Reserve Ratio (SRR) by one percentage point to 3%, effective from the reserve maintenance period beginning 9 December, 2026. The move permanently absorbs about Rs. 150 billion from the money market.

The CBSL’s target measure, Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI) inflation, rose to 8.3% in October. The CBSL projects it will reach about 9% by the end of November and stay elevated for several months. It now expects inflation to return to the 5% target in the second half of 2027, later than previously forecast. One-year-ahead inflation expectations have risen recently, while medium-term expectations remain anchored around the target, the CBSL said.

“In the short term, what we do currently may not have a significant impact on inflation, but it will have a small signalling effect and help anchor inflation expectations,” Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe told the post-Monetary Policy Review media briefing last week.

Excess liquidity in the money market stands at about Rs. 450 billion, which leaves roughly Rs. 300 billion after the SRR increase. “This is a good opportunity for us to use this instrument to absorb liquidity on a permanent basis,” Dr. Weerasinghe said.

CBSL Senior Deputy Governor Dr. Chandranath Amarasekara said: “You can think of this as SRR normalisation.”

The CBSL said the easing cycle could resume once inflation is clearly on a downward path.

title: Parliament panel calls for EV tax incentives, battery recycling rules | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:50
-     - 126

Parliament’s Committee on Ways and Means has called for tax concessions and policy incentives to promote electric vehicles (EVs), along with a proper system to manage used EV batteries, the Parliament Secretariat said.

The Committee met last week under the chairmanship of Committee on Ways and Means Chairman MP Wijesiri Basnayake. It discussed vehicle imports and the taxes on them, the promotion of EVs, and delays in clearing imported goods through Customs.

Members stressed the need to simplify tax policies so that EVs become affordable to the general public. The Committee also discussed the need to update Customs classifications and Harmonised System (HS) codes, the codes used to classify goods for Customs duty, in line with international standards, and to introduce proper quality standards for EVs and their batteries.

The Committee paid special attention to the absence of a proper system in the country for disposing of or recycling used EV batteries. Officials said importers or manufacturers should be made responsible for the proper disposal or recycling of batteries once they reach the end of their useful life.

To reduce the impact of EV charging on the national electricity grid, the Committee also discussed encouraging the use of solar power and battery energy storage systems.

On vehicle imports more broadly, the Committee examined the number and value of vehicles imported since import restrictions were relaxed, and the tax system that applies to them. It discussed the complexity of calculating taxes on imported vehicles, which depend on several factors including engine capacity, Cost, Insurance and Freight (CIF) value, and excise duty, as well as issues relating to Customs valuations.

The Committee also discussed delays in clearing imported goods caused by the need to obtain approvals from several Government institutions besides Customs. The lack of a common digital system among these institutions, including the Department of Import and Export Control, has led to delays in approvals and difficulties in coordination.

Officials said the delays result in containers being held at ports, forcing importers to bear additional costs, including storage charges. The meeting emphasised the need to strengthen coordination among the institutions involved and speed up the clearance process.

Deputy Ministers Eranga Weeraratne and Nishantha Jayaweera, MPs Ashoka Sapumal Ranwala, Dr. Nandana Millagala and Champika Hettiarachchi, and officials of Sri Lanka Customs attended the meeting.

The financing, offered following a positive assessment of the Government’s reform program and policy commitments, is intended to complement financial assistance provided by the World Bank under its Development Policy Operation.

title: Govt. seeks IMF waivers for missed targets ahead of 2 Dec. Board review | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:50
-     - 216

The Government has asked the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to waive targets it missed under its Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and to change targets for the rest of the program, an IMF notice shows. The requests will go before the Fund’s Executive Board on 2 December, 2026.

The Board will consider Sri Lanka’s review together with its Article IV consultation, the IMF’s regular health check of a member country’s economy. According to the Fund’s schedule of Board meetings, it will also consider ‘waivers of Nonobservance of Performance Criteria, Modification of Performance Criteria’. The notice did not elaborate.

Performance criteria are the binding conditions, usually quantitative targets, that a country must meet on set dates for IMF disbursements to continue. When a country misses one, the Board can grant a waiver so that the review can be completed and funds released. A modification changes the targets for future test dates, usually to reflect changed economic conditions.

The notice did not say which criteria Sri Lanka had missed or how the forward targets would be revised. The Board meeting follows the staff-level agreement on the Seventh Review that IMF staff and the Sri Lankan authorities reached on 4 October, 2026.

Board approval of the tranche was made contingent on Parliament passing a 2027 Budget in line with program parameters, along with a financing assurances review. That review confirms that creditors are providing enough debt relief and financing to keep the program on track.

title: Travellers to Sri Lanka can board flights without ETA as portal goes down | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:49
-     - 97

Sri Lanka is allowing travellers of most nationalities to board flights to the country without prior Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) approval until further notice, after its ETA application portal went offline for system maintenance.

Eligible passengers can obtain an ETA or Visit Visa from immigration authorities on arrival at the Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA) or another relevant port of entry, the Department of Immigration and Emigration said in a circular dated 23 November, 2026.

Airlines and their ground handling agents have been asked to make the necessary arrangements to board passengers covered by the temporary measure, which aims to minimise disruption to international travellers.

Citizens of the US, the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and European Union countries are among those eligible. Several Sri Lankan diplomatic missions shared the notice yesterday. They included the Embassies in the Philippines, Japan, Sweden and Türkiye and the High Commissions in Australia and Singapore.

Sri Lanka has offered free tourist ETAs to citizens of 40 countries since 25 May, 2026. However, the missions’ notices do not say whether the fee waiver extends to authorisations issued on arrival under the temporary arrangement.

title: Iconic Trust sells Rs. 1.2 b stake in Sierra Cables | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:47
-     - 114

Iconic Trust Ltd., sold 34 million Sierra Cables PLC shares for Rs. 1.2 billion on 17 November, 2026, which lifted the cable maker’s public holding by 6.33 percentage points to 49.72%, the company said.

The shares, 6.33% of Sierra Cables’ issued ordinary voting shares, were sold on the market at prices between Rs. 36.00 and Rs. 37.10, at a weighted average of Rs. 36.03 a share. The total consideration was Rs. 1,225 million before transaction costs.

Iconic Trust now holds 129.6 million shares, or 24.11% of the company.

Because the buyers fall within the Listing Rules’ definition of public shareholders, shares that were previously excluded from the public holding now count towards it. The public holding is the portion of a company’s shares held by the investing public rather than by its controlling or related shareholders. The last public holding figure Sierra Cables disclosed was 43.39%, as at 30 September, 2026. The company said it still meets the minimum public holding requirement under the Listing Rules.

Sierra Cables Directors D.S.K. Amarasekera and M.A.P.N. Weerasingha are also directors of Iconic Trust. The sale was disclosed to the Sierra Cables Board on 20 November, 2026. The shares in which each Director is deemed to have a relevant interest through Iconic Trust fell from 163.6 million to 129.6 million. A relevant interest is an indirect stake held through another entity.

title: Tokyo Cement strengthens market position to sustain growth in 2Q | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:29
-     - 97

Tokyo Cement Group (Tokyo Cement) has posted a turnover of Rs. 20.9 billion for the second quarter ending 30 September 2026, reflecting a 28% increase from Rs. 16.3 billion recorded in the corresponding period of the previous year. Profit After Tax (PAT) stood at Rs. 870 million, compared to Rs. 1 billion in the same period last year.

The increase in turnover reflects the growth in volume and price increase from the previous quarter. However, profitability remained under pressure due to elevated raw material costs and currency volatility during the period, the company said.

It said the volatile and unpredictable nature of the Iran conflict continued to cloud the economic outlook during the quarter, with frequent fluctuations in global fuel prices and the looming threat of complete disruption of diesel supply weighing heavy on consumer confidence. These uncertainties, compounded by rising energy costs and climate-related risks, contributed to a more cautious investment climate and moderated economic momentum during the quarter.

The domestic economy faced mounting cost pressures, with fuel and energy expenditure rising sharply alongside a global fertiliser shortage, and the potential impact of severe El Niño conditions on the agriculture sector. Over the quarter, the Rupee was observed to depreciate against the US Dollar increasing pressures on reserves. Furthermore, year-on-year headline inflation, measured by the National Consumer Price Index (NCPI) reached 8.1% in August, exceeding the Central Bank’s target range for a second consecutive month.

Despite these headwinds, several indicators pointed to continued resilience in the external sector. Gross official reserves increased, supported by improved revenue collection and prudent Government expenditure, while export earnings and worker remittances sustained foreign exchange inflows despite subdued global demand and rising shipping costs. Tourism earnings also showed signs of recovery ahead of the peak season. Against this backdrop of heightened global and climate-related uncertainty, the Central Bank decided to maintain the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) at 8.75% throughout the July to September quarter.

Further reinforcing investor confidence, Fitch Ratings upgraded Sri Lanka’s credit rating to ‘B-’ with a Stable Outlook, citing stronger-than-expected fiscal and external sector performance. This marked a notable improvement from the ‘CCC+’ rating assigned since November 2020, signaling progress in the country’s economic recovery.

Against this mixed macroeconomic backdrop, Sri Lanka’s cement industry moved to strengthen market resilience by maintaining uninterrupted supply and stable market prices despite significant increases in raw material, freight, insurance and fuel costs. Cement consumption continued its upward trajectory during the quarter, supported by favourable weather conditions and the availability of construction materials. The Sri Lanka Purchasing Managers’ Index for Construction (PMI-Construction) also indicated continued industry expansion with new orders stemming from State-led development projects, although supply chain disruptions in the Middle East constrained the availability of bitumen, required for road construction activities. 

Tokyo Cement Group further strengthened its market position during the quarter, gaining market share as coastal shipping improved access to the Western Province and beyond. The expanded market reach supported higher utilisation of the Group’s enhanced production capacity, driving greater operational efficiency.

However, as a result of currency depreciation and global cost increases, all material inputs, both locally manufactured and imported, increased in price, thereby softening investment sentiment among private developers and individual investors. These pressures also threatened to further impede the implementation of public sector development projects.

As the financial sector anticipates a moderation in private sector credit growth over the coming quarters, the trajectory of the Middle East conflict, global energy prices and supply chain conditions will remain critical determinants of national economic momentum and sectoral growth prospects.

Against this backdrop, the sovereign credit rating upgrade represents a significant positive development, with the potential to strengthen investor confidence and attract diversified foreign currency inflows. Despite persistent external shocks, the national economic outlook remains broadly stable, underpinned by sustained fiscal revenue and steady forex remittances. However, elevated import costs and a slower-than-anticipated recovery in tourism continue to pose near-term challenges, while geopolitical tensions and weather-related uncertainties remain key downside risks.

Realising the economy’s growth potential will depend on timely execution of public sector infrastructure projects and the policy direction set out in the forthcoming November budget. Together, these will be instrumental in translating improving macroeconomic confidence into tangible economic activity and investment.

Within this broader context, the construction sector maintains a cautiously optimistic outlook, supported by infrastructure development initiatives already underway by regional Government institutes. Sustaining this momentum will depend on the timely commencement and implementation of planned large-scale public investment projects, alongside an enabling policy environment that encourages private sector participation and reinforces investor confidence.

Tokyo Cement maintains a conservative short- to medium-term outlook, while remaining confident in the country’s economic fundamentals. With an enhanced production capacity the Group is well positioned to capitalise on future industry growth. Tokyo Cement will continue to exercise strict cost discipline, safeguard stakeholder interests, and play an active role in supporting the country’s construction-led economic recovery, the company said.

title: Deloitte Sri Lanka examines Budget 2027 as nation looks beyond stabilisation towards sustainable growth | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:28
-     - 102

As Sri Lanka moves beyond economic stabilisation towards its next phase of growth, attention is turning to how fiscal reforms, investment priorities and policy initiatives can translate into meaningful economic progress. Bringing together perspectives from Government, industry and economic policy, Deloitte Sri Lanka hosted its Budget 2027 webinar, “Beyond Stabilization: Building for Growth,” on 12 November, 2026, following the presentation of the National Budget in Parliament.

The webinar provided a platform for policymakers, economists and business leaders to examine the Budget through two complementary discussions, “Fiscal Perspective” and “Trade & Economy.” Moderated by Partner and Head of Tax Charmaine Tillekeratne and Head of Strategy, Risk & Transactions Ruvini Fernando, respectively, the sessions explored the implications of fiscal measures, investment, trade, energy and economic reforms. The discussions highlighted the importance of moving beyond policy announcements towards effective implementation and tangible outcomes for businesses and the wider economy.

Budget 2027 reflects Sri Lanka’s continued emphasis on fiscal discipline while seeking to create greater opportunities for investment and economic expansion. According to Budget 2027, the Government targets a primary surplus of 2.3% of GDP and an overall fiscal deficit of 4.5% in 2027, with tax revenue projected at 14.6% of GDP. Total budgeted revenue stands at Rs. 6.15 trillion against an expenditure of Rs. 7.93 trillion, reflecting the continued importance of balancing fiscal commitments with national development priorities.

Taxation remains a key area of focus, with proposals aimed at providing relief to individuals, encouraging investment and strengthening the tax framework. The proposed increase in annual personal income tax relief from Rs. 1.8 million to Rs. 1.95 million, together with revised progressive tax bands, is expected to reduce the tax burden on qualifying individuals. For businesses, the proposed 200% enhanced capital allowance for qualifying BOI-approved investments of at least $ 3 million in export-oriented manufacturing and tourism introduces a further incentive for investment in priority sectors.

Other notable measures include the proposed expansion of capital gains tax coverage to certain digital assets and commercial rights, legal recognition of electronic VAT invoices and changes to VAT refund eligibility for new exporters. The proposed abolition of the Tourism Development Levy from April 2027 also forms part of the Budget’s revenue-related measures.

Beyond taxation, public investment and private-sector development feature prominently in the Government’s growth agenda. Budget 2027 allocates Rs. 2 trillion for public investment, with substantial provisions for highways, railways, healthcare, irrigation and water supply. Support for micro, small and medium enterprises also remains a priority, with Rs. 67.69 billion allocated towards interest subsidies and bank refinancing to support Rs. 174 billion in concessionary lending.

The importance of these measures was reflected in Deloitte’s webinar discussions, where panellists examined the challenges of improving access to finance, strengthening investment facilitation and reducing administrative barriers. The conversations highlighted that financial allocations alone may not be sufficient without stronger institutional capabilities and practical mechanisms to support implementation.

Energy security, digital transformation and governance reforms represent further priorities within Budget 2027. Proposed initiatives relating to renewable energy, efficient power markets and digital infrastructure sit alongside plans to strengthen investment protection, public-private partnerships and State-owned enterprise management. The anticipated Digital Economy Bill and proposed Cyber Security Authority also reflect the increasing importance of digital governance in Sri Lanka’s economic development.

The wider discussion on trade and the economy also drew attention to power-sector efficiency, particularly the need to achieve a lower unit cost of electricity and address policy challenges that influence business competitiveness over the longer term.

Taken together, Budget 2027 outlines a range of fiscal and structural measures intended to support Sri Lanka’s transition towards sustainable growth. Their longer-term significance will depend on effective implementation, institutional co-ordination and the ability to translate policy priorities into meaningful economic outcomes.

title: Sri Lanka must use foreign policy to protect Palestinian rights: Sajith | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:44
-     - 30

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa on Monday urged the Government to use Sri Lanka’s foreign policy to protect the rights of Palestinians and to support a two-State solution under which Israel and Palestine live side by side in peace.

Speaking in Parliament, Premadasa said Sri Lanka must champion the cause of human rights.

“We must ensure that the rights of the Palestinians who are suffering in the West Bank and Gaza are protected,” he said.

He said Sri Lanka should support the existing international agreement on two States living side by side in a peaceful and harmonious environment. He referred to United Nations Resolutions 242 and 338 and said they had been reinforced by later international accords, including the Abraham Accords and the Camp David Accords, as well as other unanimous conclusions reached by the international community.

“We must ensure that through our foreign policy the genocide in Gaza and the West Bank is stopped. We must protect the rights of the Palestinians and also ensure that the two States, Israel and Palestine, live in harmony and conduct their State activities through peaceful approaches,” Premadasa said.

He listed the protection of human rights and democratic values, together with respect for international law, as two of the 12 pillars on which he said Sri Lanka’s foreign policy should be judged.

“We must ensure that we respect international laws, international organisations, international conventions, customs and practices,” he said.

title: Cabinet moves to amend Act to address difficulties in functioning of Language Institute’s Board | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:43
-     - 21

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved a proposal to amend the National Language Education and Training Institute Act, No. 26 of 2007, in order to address practical difficulties in the functioning of the institute’s Management Board.

Under the Act, the Secretaries to the Ministries in charge of Education, Public Administration, Finance, and Constitutional Affairs and National Integration serve as ex officio members of the Management Board of the National Language Education and Training Institute. However, it has been observed that the busy schedules of these senior officials make it difficult for them to take part in the Board’s monthly meetings.

To resolve the issue, the Cabinet has approved a proposal made by the Justice and National Integration Minister Harshana Nanayakkara, instructing the Legal Draftsman to prepare a draft bill amending the relevant sections of the Act.

The amendments are intended to allow arrangements to be made for the appointment of ex officio members to the Management Board in a manner that minimises these problems.

title: Cabinet green lights new building complex for Puttalam District Secretariat | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 25 November 2026 05:42
-     - 25

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved the construction of a new building complex for the Puttalam District Secretariat, including a four-storey office building, a 1,000-seat auditorium and a parking area.

The new complex will be built within the premises where the existing Secretariat is located.

A building complex consisting of three sections was first proposed for the Puttalam District Secretariat in 2013. To date, however, only its southern four-storey building has been constructed.

Due to insufficient space and facilities in that building, divisions of the office have had to be maintained at various locations. This has hindered the coordination of administrative activities and the direct supervision of operations by the District Secretary.

Constructing a building complex equipped with modern facilities has therefore been identified as a priority. The objectives are to establish office divisions formally under one roof, strengthen administrative coordination, facilitate public services, and provide adequate facilities for district-level meetings and conferences.

The proposal to this effect was submitted by Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Minister Prof. A.H.M.H. Abayarathna.
